ENERGY-NEGOTIATIONS WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA ON PRICING AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been over seven months since the National Energy Program was bestowed upon the nation by the federal government in Ottawa. The oil industry and the producing provinces responded to it at the time with consternation, outrage and alarm, but the federal Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) confidentially reassured us that he had come to expect that kind of emotional reaction from the provinces and the oil industry. He said that very soon both the industry and the provinces would come to accept the new arrangements and that everything would return to normal. Now let us see what has happened since he gave us the National Energy Program. What does he consider normal? Here are a few symptoms.
First, oil and gas exploration activity in the western provinces has been reduced by more than half. Three thousand of the 20,000 men employed in the trade have been laid off by mid-May and another 6,000 are expected to be laid off by mid-summer. Where 370 rigs were drilling last year, 177 are drilling this year; 131 rigs have left the country. In short, an industry upon which both the economy and security of the country depend has been thrust into a depression.
Second, development of the heavy oil and tar sands plants has been brought to a hald, although there is enough synthetic oil in Alberta to meet the needs of Canada for 300 years at present rates of production.
Third, Alberta has reduced its supply of crude oil to central Canada and will cut back the supply by 15 per cent by the end of September.
Fourth, nearly $1.5 billion is being sent to Belgium to pay for the Petrofina Oil Company as a federal gift to Petro-Canada, an expenditure which will directly raise the price of gasoline and at the same time will not add a single barrel of oil to Canada's supply.
Fifth, per capita consumption of oil in Canada continues to rise because the National Energy Program holds Canadian prices far below prices charged in nearly all countries in the western world, in fact at about one-third the price charged in Great Britain which is self-sufficient in oil because of the North Sea developments. In the United States, by contrast, higher prices have had the effect of reducing imports by 24 per cent in a single year and cutting consumption by two million barrels a day. Meanwhile American cars stream over the border to fill up on Canada's cut rate gasoline.
Sixth, heavy oil wells in the Lloydminster area are shutting down because the National Energy Program does not provide enough money to keep them operating.
Seventh, unemployment stalks Ontario industry which is being deprived of machinery and equipment orders due to the cutback in Alberta conventional oil and gas exploration and the arrest of tar sands development.
June 16, 1981

Eighth, British Columbia and Saskatchewan have defied the federal government and refused to pay the tax it is attempting to levy on natural gas production. Nova Scotia and Newfoundland have announced they will not recognize federal laws leasing oil rights on offshore lands, a situation that could conceivably see both levels of government leasing the same properties. In the meantime, Alberta has set up three gas wells of its own and claimed the right to export gas to the United States without federal interference and the Alberta court of appeal has unanimously upheld the position of the province.
Ninth, the United States government is considering triggering the provisions of the United States mineral lands leasing act against Canadian oil and mining companies operating in the United States as a retaliation against the National Energy Program Canadianization measures, a move which would maim or bankrupt hundreds of Canadian resource companies operating in the United States.
In other words, the National Energy Program after seven months has managed to cripple the Canadian exploration industry and to drive it out of the country, to increase Canadian oil consumption, to disrupt the supply of existing oil, to ship millions upon millions of dollars overseas, to jeopardize relations with the Americans, to expose us far more to dependence on Arab oil, to halt development of the tar sands, to throw federal-provincial relations into chaos bordering on legal civil war, and to find no oil. All that in seven months!
This also means, moreover, that the reassurances of the federal minister of energy that everything would return to normal have turned out to be dead wrong. Apparently he had no idea whatever of the damage he was about to wreak upon his country. It was a case of too much power exercised in both arrogance and ignorance with calamitous consequence to the industry and the nation whose ill fortune it was to have been left in his hands. That is what history will write beneath the name of the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
